newsitem.title: UK: Copper bruised on LME, hits 4-1/2 month lows.
newsitem.headline: Copper bruised on LME, hits 4-1/2 month lows.

text.p: Copper prices sought to stabilise during Wednesday's LME ring and kerb sessions, having earlier been hammered to 4-1/2 month lows, although the market was still substantially lower at the recess.
Traders said copper market sentiment was now "on the turn" after Tuesday's late declines and the followthrough seen early today.
"Most of the damage was done overnight. There was a little bit of profit-taking (purchases) in the rings, but I still see it going to $2,200," one trader said.

Since concluding Tuesday's kerb at $2,368, prices have been buffeted by waves of fund sales, speculative liquidation, and option-related hedge selling. The decline - modest at first - has reflected rising stocks and expectations that further inventory increases will be large.
LME warehouse stocks are expected to be swelled by deliveries into the U.S., Europe and the Far East in coming weeks, they said.

The only mitigating factor in the short-term is the July tightness. although spreads covering July were softer, with July/August at $84 against $99 on Tuesday, some shorts have been rolled forward into August, other traders noted.
Last three months trade was at $2,271 a tonne, which was some $20 below the late Tuesday close.

Activity in the rest of the metals, including aluminium, was relatively low-key, and some metals started to edge back into the plus column once the early copper-related mark-down did not result in actual selling.
"Aluminium does not look good, and people do want to short it now, but the others do not really justify a sell-off," another trader said.
Aluminium did manage to stave off a test of expected sell-stops in the $1,530/40 area by rebounding from $1,545, although final trade was at $1,563, still down $2.

Traders said a 950-tonne stock fall was smaller than some recent declines, which also underlined negative sentiment. On Thursday, the IPAI releases producer inventory data for May, although this may equally do little for the market.
"At the moment, nobody is paying any attention to stocks. Consumers are not buying, and the funds are looking to sell," a trader said.
Zinc, which only last week was at 6-3/4 year highs near $1,500, initially buckled, but managed to climb back above $1,450 - an intermediate chart level. Last trade was at $1,456, still down $4.
Lead similarly fell away in early trading before recovering to regain the $650 area. Prices were just $1 higher at the end of the kerb at $650.

Nickel, which received a brief boost from Tuesday's Falconbridge strike vote, reverted to the downside on Wednesday, depressed by rising stocks and reasonable Russian shipments. Three months closed the kerb at $6,890, down $45 from Tuesday.
Tin managed to avert a re-test of the $5,490 2-1/4 year lows hit last week by again picking up some trade support just above $5,500. Final trade was at $5,530, just $10 lower.
Alloy was marked down with primary, and was quoted at $1,415/25 a tonne, down some $12 from yesterday.
